definition: The way of describing data that E. F. Codd proposed in 1970: all data is held as relations (sets of tuples), with no pointers and no visible storage order, and queried with set-based operators. SQL databases are built on it, with some deviations.
example: Postgres, MySQL and SQLite are all descendants of the relational model.

definition: In the relational model, a set of tuples that all share the same heading of named, typed attributes. Informally it is a table, but a relation has no duplicate rows, no row order and no column order.
example: Student(sid, name, year) holding three students is a relation of degree 3 and cardinality 3.

definition: One element of a relation: a value for each attribute in the heading. It corresponds to a row in SQL and is read as one true fact.
example: (2, Ben, 1) in Student(sid, name, year) states "student 2 is called Ben and is in year 1".

definition: The set of (attribute name, domain) pairs that every tuple of a relation conforms to. Because it is a set, attributes are identified by name, not by position.
example: The heading of Student is {(sid, INTEGER), (name, TEXT), (year, INTEGER)}.

definition: The set of values an attribute is allowed to take, similar to a column type plus any rules on it. A domain constraint says every stored value must come from its attribute's domain.
example: The year column can require a value with NOT NULL and restrict it to integers one through four with CHECK (year BETWEEN 1 AND 4).

definition: The number of attributes in a relation's heading. It changes only when the schema changes, not when rows are inserted or deleted.
example: Course(cid, title, dept, credits) has degree 4 however many courses it holds.

definition: Interpreting absence as false relative to a relation assumed complete for its stated predicate. A query can establish that no stored holiday booking exists; concluding anything about actual attendance requires additional domain facts.
example: With no row (42, 2026-03-03) in holiday, the database is asserting that employee 42 had no holiday booked that day.

definition: Insulating programs from changes in how data is organised. Physical data independence means storage changes (indexes, file layout) do not break queries; logical data independence means changes to tables can be hidden behind views so applications keep working.
example: Adding an index to a Postgres table speeds queries up without changing any of them: physical data independence.

definition: A set of attributes whose values are unique across every tuple a relation could legally contain. Adding attributes to a superkey always gives another superkey; a candidate key is a superkey with nothing extra.
example: In Employee(emp_id, email, name, dept), {emp_id, name} is a superkey but not a candidate key.

definition: A minimal superkey: a set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples in every legal state, from which no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness. A relation can have several; one is chosen as the primary key.
example: Employee has two candidate keys, {emp_id} and {email}.

definition: A candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. In SQL it is normally enforced with UNIQUE plus NOT NULL on its columns.
example: If emp_id is the primary key, {email} is an alternate key.

definition: The rule that no attribute of a primary key may be NULL, so every tuple can be identified and referred to.
example: PostgreSQL PRIMARY KEY implies NOT NULL on its columns; some ordinary SQLite rowid-table primary keys historically permit NULL unless separately excluded.

definition: The rule that every foreign-key value either matches an existing key value in the referenced relation or, where allowed, is NULL. It prevents references to rows that do not exist.
example: Deleting a student who still has enrolments fails under the default ON DELETE NO ACTION.

definition: The rule that no two tuples of a relation may agree on all attributes of a candidate key.
example: PRIMARY KEY (sid, cid) on enrolled stops one student enrolling on the same course twice.

definition: A pre-relational database in which programs reach records by following pointers from one record to the next along fixed access paths. Changing the storage structure could break the programs.
example: IBM's IMS (hierarchical) and CODASYL (network) systems of the 1960s and 1970s were navigational.

definition: IBM's Information Management System, a hierarchical navigational database from the late 1960s. Records form parent–child trees that programs walk along.
example: An IMS program might get a part, then its first child supplier, then the next child supplier.

definition: The Conference on Data Systems Languages, whose database task group described a network model using navigable links among record types. The relational model instead exposes value-based relations and operations to applications.
A database that stores records in parent–child trees, each child having exactly one parent. IBM's IMS is the best-known example.
The IBM researcher who proposed the relational model in his 1970 paper A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks.
An IBM relational-database research system from the 1970s, used to develop SQL and influential cost-based query optimisation techniques.
A relational database research project at the University of California, Berkeley, from the 1970s. Its successor research project, Postgres, became PostgreSQL.
IBM’s commercial relational database, announced in 1983 and developed from relational database research including System R.
A collection like a set but allowed to hold the same element more than once. SQL tables and query results are bags, which is why duplicates appear unless a key or DISTINCT prevents them.
example: SELECT dept FROM emp returns one row per employee, repeating each department name.

definition: A PostgreSQL system column holding a row version's physical location (block number and position in the block). It can tell identical duplicate rows apart, but changes when a row is updated or the table is rewritten, so it is not a stable identifier.
example: DELETE FROM page_views WHERE ctid = '(0,2)' removes exactly one of two identical rows.

definition: An internal locator for a stored row version, such as PostgreSQL's ctid (page number and position). It can change after an update or table rewrite and is unsuitable as a stable application reference; a SQLite rowid is an integer table key rather than a physical page address.
A SQLite table option that stores the table organised by its declared primary key instead of a hidden integer rowid. Such tables require a PRIMARY KEY, and its columns are NOT NULL.

The PostgreSQL maintenance operation that reclaims space taken by dead row versions so it can be reused. It runs automatically through autovacuum; it can also change the physical order rows are later read in.
A foreign-key action: when the referenced row is deleted (or its key updated), the referencing columns are set to their column defaults.
Database management system: the software that stores data and runs queries against it, such as PostgreSQL, Oracle or SQLite.
The person responsible for running a database: its structure, performance, backups and access.
International Business Machines, the company whose researchers developed the relational model and the System R database project.

Operators on relations that return relations, so finite expressions can be composed from them. Ordinary relational algebra expresses a large class of queries, but cannot express unbounded graph reachability without a recursive extension.
example: π name (σ cid='DB' (Student ⋈ Enrolled)) lists the students on course DB.

definition: The relational-algebra operator, written with the Greek letter σ (sigma), that keeps only the tuples satisfying a condition. It filters rows and corresponds to SQL's WHERE, not to SELECT.
example: σ year=2 (Student) keeps the students in year 2.

definition: The relational-algebra operator, written with the Greek letter π (pi), that keeps only the listed attributes and removes duplicate tuples. It corresponds to SQL's SELECT DISTINCT column list.
example: π cid (Enrolled) gives {DB, OS, LA}: three tuples from six enrolments.

definition: The relational-algebra operator, written with the Greek letter ρ (rho), that gives a relation or attribute a new name. It is needed to join a relation with a copy of itself.
example: ρ S1 (Student) × ρ S2 (Student) pairs every student with every student, with attributes S1.sid, S2.sid and so on.

definition: Two relations are union-compatible when they have the same attributes with the same domains, which union, difference and intersection require.
example: π sid (Student) and π sid (Enrolled) are union-compatible; Student and Enrolled are not.

definition: The relational-algebra operator R − S that returns the tuples of R that do not appear in S. Both inputs must be union-compatible, and order matters: R − S is not the same as S − R. It is one of the primitive operators. SQL writes it EXCEPT, which removes duplicates unless EXCEPT ALL is used.
example: Every student id minus the student ids that appear in Enrolled leaves the students with no enrolment.

definition: The relational-algebra operator R ∩ S that returns the tuples present in both of two union-compatible relations. It is not primitive: it equals R − (R − S). SQL writes it INTERSECT, which removes duplicates unless INTERSECT ALL is used.
example: The students on DB intersected with the students on AI gives the students taking both.

definition: A join written R ⋈θ S that pairs tuples of R and S satisfying a condition θ (theta). It is defined as a Cartesian product followed by a selection.
example: Joining orders to price bands on order.total BETWEEN band.low AND band.high is a theta join.

definition: A theta join whose condition uses only equality comparisons. Most joins written in SQL are equijoins.
example: student JOIN enrolled ON student.sid = enrolled.sid is an equijoin.

definition: The relational-algebra operator R ⋉ S, which returns the tuples of R that have at least one matching tuple in S, keeping only R's attributes. SQL expresses it with WHERE EXISTS or IN.
example: Students ⋉ Enrolled gives the students with at least one enrolment, each once.

definition: The relational-algebra operator R ▷ S, which returns the tuples of R that have no matching tuple in S. SQL expresses it with WHERE NOT EXISTS.
example: Student ▷ Enrolled gives Dev, the one student with no enrolments.

definition: A query language is relationally complete if it can express every query that relational algebra can. SQL is, and goes further with aggregation, ordering and recursion.

The relational-algebra operator R ÷ S answering "for all" questions: it returns the values of R's other attributes that are paired in R with every tuple of S. It is derived from projection, product and difference.
example: Enrolled ÷ π cid (σ dept='CS' (Course)) gives the students taking every CS course.

definition: In relational division R ÷ S, the right-hand relation S: the set every qualifying result must be paired with. If it is empty, every candidate qualifies vacuously.
example: In "students taking every CS course", the divisor relation is {DB, OS}.

definition: A rule stating that two relational-algebra expressions always give the same result, whatever the relations contain. Optimisers use these rules to replace a query with a cheaper equivalent.
example: σ p (R ⋈ S) ≡ σ p (R) ⋈ S when p mentions only R's attributes.

definition: Transforming a query into a different but equivalent form, using algebraic equivalences, so that it can run more cheaply. It is the first half of query optimisation; choosing among the alternatives by estimated cost is the second.
example: Moving a WHERE filter below a join so the join sees 1,000 rows instead of 200,000.

definition: A query optimiser that generates equivalent plans and picks the one with the lowest estimated cost, using statistics about the data such as row counts and value distributions.
example: PostgreSQL's planner is cost-based: it estimates the cost of a hash join versus a nested loop and chooses the cheaper.

definition: The extended relational-algebra operator, written with the Greek letter γ (gamma), that groups tuples by some attributes and computes aggregates per group. It corresponds to SQL's GROUP BY and is not part of Codd's original algebra.
example: γ year, COUNT(sid) (Student) counts students per year.

definition: A "for all" statement is vacuously true when there is nothing to check: a claim about every member of an empty set cannot fail.
example: If department X has no courses, "student takes every X course" is true for every student.

definition: A relational-algebra expression drawn as a tree: leaves are stored relations, inner nodes are operators, and data flows from the leaves up to the root.
The SQL module of Apache Spark, a distributed data-processing engine. Its Catalyst optimiser applies rule-based and cost-based rewrites to query plans.
The left-hand side of a functional dependency: the set of attributes whose values fix the values on the right.
example: In cid → ctitle, cid is the determinant.

definition: A functional dependency X → Y in which Y is a subset of X, so it holds in every relation and says nothing. Non-trivial FDs are the ones that record real business rules.
example: {sid, cid} → cid is trivial; sid → sname is not.

definition: Three inference rules for functional dependencies, published by William Armstrong in 1974: reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity. They are sound and complete: they derive exactly the FDs that logically follow.
example: From A → B and B → C, transitivity gives A → C.

definition: Armstrong's first axiom: if Y is a subset of X, then X → Y. It produces exactly the trivial functional dependencies.
Armstrong's second axiom: if X → Y, then XZ → YZ for any set Z. Adding the same attributes to both sides keeps a dependency true.
example: From sid → sname, augmentation gives {sid, cid} → {sname, cid}.

definition: Armstrong's third axiom: if X → Y and Y → Z, then X → Z. Chains of dependencies like this are what make transitive dependencies and closures matter.
example: oid → cid and cid → cname give oid → cname.

definition: A rule derived from Armstrong's axioms: if X → Y and X → Z, then X → YZ.
A rule derived from Armstrong's axioms: if X → YZ, then X → Y and X → Z. It splits right-hand sides only; a left-hand side cannot be split.
A rule derived from Armstrong's axioms: if X → Y and WY → Z, then WX → Z.
example: From A → B and BC → D, pseudotransitivity gives AC → D.

definition: Inference rules are sound when every conclusion follows from the premises, and complete when every conclusion that follows can be derived. Armstrong’s rules have both properties for functional dependencies over ordinary relations.

term: Closure of a set of FDs (F⁺)
definition: The set of every functional dependency implied by a set F, written F⁺. It can be exponentially large, so in practice you compute attribute closures instead of listing it.

The set of all attributes that an attribute set X determines under a set of functional dependencies, written X⁺. It is computed by repeatedly applying any FD whose left side is already in the set. X is a superkey exactly when X⁺ contains every attribute.
example: With A → B, B → C and CD → E, the attribute closure of {A, D} is {A, B, C, D, E}.

definition: A state that a repeated step no longer changes. A fixpoint loop keeps applying its step until the result stops changing, as the attribute-closure algorithm does.
An attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key. Normal-form tests need every candidate key, because an attribute can be prime through an alternate candidate key.
example: In Teaching(student, course, teacher), with keys {student, course} and {student, teacher}, all three attributes are prime.

definition: An equivalent set of functional dependencies with single-attribute right sides, no extraneous determinant attributes and no redundant dependencies. Some texts group dependencies sharing a determinant into a canonical cover; minimal covers need not be unique.
example: {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C} has minimal cover {A → B, B → C}.

definition: An attribute on either side of a functional dependency that can be removed from that side while keeping the entire FD set equivalent. In a singleton-right-side minimal cover, the useful reductions remove extraneous determinant attributes.
example: In AB → C with A → B also present, B is extraneous: A → C already follows.

definition: A functional dependency that can be derived from the others in its set, so removing it changes nothing.
example: A → C is redundant alongside A → B and B → C.

definition: The hardest problems in the class NP: no polynomial-time algorithm is known for any of them, and one for any would give one for all. Deciding whether an attribute is prime, that is in some candidate key, is NP-complete, which is why the 3NF test can be expensive in theory.
Analysing existing data to discover its structure, such as value ranges, uniqueness and candidate functional dependencies. What it finds are hypotheses for a human to confirm, not rules.

A running-time upper bound given by a fixed power of the encoded input size. This is a useful theoretical distinction from exponential growth, rather than a promise that every polynomial algorithm is fast in practice.
example: The attribute-closure algorithm is polynomial in the number of attributes and FDs.

definition: A condition on a relation's functional (and other) dependencies that rules out a particular kind of redundancy. The common ones form a ladder: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, 5NF, each stricter than the last.
A problem caused by storing one fact in many rows: an update that changes some copies but not all leaves the data contradicting itself. Normalisation removes it by storing each fact once.
example: Ann's name repeated on every order line, and a rename that misses one line.

definition: Being unable to record one fact without also recording an unrelated one, because the facts share a table and its key.
example: In a single order-line table, a new product cannot be recorded until someone orders it.

definition: Losing one fact as a side effect of deleting another, because both were stored in the same rows.
example: Deleting Raj's only order also deletes the fact that customer C9 is called Raj.

definition: A single value from a chosen attribute domain in the relational presentation. The classical flat model excludes repeating collections as attribute values, but the mere ability to inspect parts of text or a date does not make those values non-atomic.
example: Under the flat phone-number domain chosen in this module, store the two phone numbers as separate contact/phone tuples rather than one collection. Searching a text component alone does not decide atomicity.

definition: A repeated collection of facts packed into one record, such as a list of phone numbers or fixed genre1, genre2 and genre3 slots. Separate owner/value tuples avoid arbitrary limits and allow ordinary per-value keys and references; SQL arrays remain valid SQL values.

A relation in first normal form is in 2NF when no non-prime attribute is determined by a proper subset of any candidate key. For ordinary schemas without constant non-prime attributes, partial dependency requires a composite key; the general definition includes the empty subset.
example: OrderLine(oid, pid, …, cname) breaks 2NF because oid alone determines cname.

definition: A relation in first normal form is in 3NF when each non-trivial single-attribute functional dependency either has a superkey determinant or has a prime right-hand attribute. Prime means belonging to at least one candidate key.
example: Order(oid, odate, cid, cname) breaks 3NF through oid → cid → cname.

definition: Boyce–Codd normal form: a relation is in BCNF when the left side of every non-trivial functional dependency is a superkey. It is stricter than 3NF and differs from it only when candidate keys overlap.
example: Teaching(student, course, teacher) with teacher → course is in 3NF but not BCNF.

definition: A normal form that removes redundancy from independent multivalued dependencies: every non-trivial multivalued dependency must have a superkey on its left.
example: (emp, skill, language) is split into (emp, skill) and (emp, language).

definition: A normal form that removes redundancy from join dependencies: a relation is in 5NF when every join dependency on it is implied by its candidate keys.

A dependency on a proper subset of a determinant, rather than on that whole determinant. In the 2NF test the determinant is a candidate key and the dependent attribute is non-prime; the general test also includes an empty subset determining a constant.
example: With key {oid, pid}, oid → odate is a partial dependency.

definition: An indirect functional dependency: the key determines X and X determines A, where X is not a superkey. Third normal form forbids it when A is non-prime.
example: oid → cid and cid → cname make cname transitively dependent on oid.

definition: A row produced by joining the parts of a bad decomposition that was never in the original relation.
example: Splitting Teaching on course and rejoining invents (Ann, DB, Jones).

definition: A decomposition is lossless if joining projections of every legal original relation reconstructs it exactly. For a binary decomposition under functional dependencies alone, this holds exactly when the shared attributes determine every attribute of at least one part.
example: Teaching split into (teacher, course) and (student, teacher) is lossless because teacher → course.

definition: A decomposition preserves dependencies when the functional dependencies that fit inside its parts together imply all the original ones, so every rule can be checked one table at a time without a join.
example: BCNF decomposition of Teaching loses {student, course} → teacher, so it is not dependency-preserving.

definition: Replacing one relation by several smaller relations over subsets of its attributes. Normalisation algorithms decompose to remove redundancy while aiming to keep the join lossless and the dependencies checkable.
example: The BCNF algorithm splits S on a violating X into X⁺ ∩ S and X ∪ (S − X⁺).

definition: An algorithm (Bernstein, 1976) that builds a 3NF schema from a minimal cover: one relation per left-hand side, plus a key relation if needed. The result is always lossless and dependency-preserving.
A dependency X ↠ Y meaning that each X value determines a set of Y values independently of the other attributes. Fourth normal form removes redundancy caused by such dependencies.
example: emp ↠ skill when an employee's skills have nothing to do with their languages.

definition: A constraint that a relation always equals the natural join of certain projections of it. Fifth normal form deals with join dependencies that do not follow from the keys.
A candidate key made of more than one attribute. When two such keys share an attribute (overlapping candidate keys), 3NF and BCNF can differ.

aliases: the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key
definition: A mnemonic that non-key facts should depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. Use precise functional-dependency and prime-attribute definitions to decide 3NF, because the slogan does not express all its cases.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the query can be answered from the index alone. PostgreSQL adds extra non-key columns with INCLUDE.
example: CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total) lets a per-customer total query use an index-only scan.

definition: A PostgreSQL plan that can return requested column values from an index. It checks the visibility map and may still fetch heap pages to establish visibility, so “index-only” does not promise zero heap fetches.

PostgreSQL table storage containing row versions in pages without a guaranteed logical order. Indexes point to row locations; a standard build uses eight-kibibyte pages, but the page size is a build-time setting.
An application pattern that runs one query to fetch a list and then one more query per item, so N items cost N + 1 round trips. Fetching everything with one join or IN query fixes it.
example: Loading 100 orders and then each order's customer separately makes 101 queries.

definition: Transactions waiting for each other because they need the same lock. A single frequently updated row (a hot row) makes every writer queue behind the one holding its lock.
example: Every comment on a viral post updating the same comment_count row.

definition: A lock on a single row. In PostgreSQL an UPDATE locks each row it changes until its transaction commits or rolls back, so a second writer to the same row waits.
A counter split across several rows (shards) so that concurrent increments usually hit different rows; reading it means summing the shards.
example: Sixteen counter rows provide sixteen row-lock targets; random choices still collide and do not guarantee sixteenfold throughput.

definition: A table of precomputed aggregates, such as daily sales per product, kept so reports read a small table instead of scanning millions of rows.
Updating a materialised view by applying only the changes to its base tables, rather than recomputing the whole query. Core PostgreSQL does not do this; the pg_ivm extension adds it.
A PostgreSQL extension that provides incrementally maintained materialised views.
Oracle's incremental refresh of a materialised view, which uses logs of changes to the base tables. It applies only to queries meeting certain restrictions.
A SQL Server view with a unique clustered index, which stores its result and keeps it up to date as the base tables change. Many query features are not allowed in it.
A database designed for analysis and reporting over large volumes of historical data, usually loaded in batches from operational systems.
A warehouse design with one central fact table of measurements joined to several denormalised dimension tables, so analytical queries need only a few joins.
example: fact_sales joined to dim_date, dim_store, dim_product and dim_customer.

definition: A table recording facts at a specified level of detail, such as one sale, one daily stock snapshot or one membership event. Facts often include numeric measures and references to dimensions; some tables record only that an event or relationship exists, without a numeric measure.
A table in a star schema describing the context of facts, such as product, store or date, usually wide and denormalised.
example: dim_product holds product, category and department names in one row.

definition: A variant of the star schema in which dimension tables are normalised into further tables, trading extra joins for less redundancy.
example: dim_product → dim_category → dim_department.

definition: Storing a table column by column rather than row by row, so analytical queries read only the columns they need and compress well.
A popular document database that stores JSON-like documents; related data is often embedded in one document rather than joined.

Amazon's managed key–value and document database. Its native query API has no relational join operation, so designs often store several entity types in one table, keyed for the queries the application needs.

A database that stores structured documents as records, often with nested objects and arrays. Embedding related data can simplify reads; document stores may also support references and join-like operations.
A DynamoDB modelling pattern that stores several entity types in one table, with keys chosen so one query fetches related items together.
example: One query returns a customer item and its recent order items because they share a partition key.

definition: A specific way an application reads or writes data, such as "get a customer's last 10 orders". NoSQL designs are built around a known list of them.

A stored generated column is computed on row writes and persisted; a virtual generated column is evaluated when read. PostgreSQL 16–17 support stored columns; PostgreSQL 18 added virtual columns and made that kind the default when the kind is omitted.
In PostgreSQL, a function or expression that always gives the same result for the same inputs, forever. Generated columns and index expressions must be immutable; current_date is not.
Change data capture: reading a database's committed changes, often from its write-ahead log, and streaming them to other systems such as search indexes or caches.
example: Debezium reads PostgreSQL's logical replication stream and publishes each change as an event.

definition: A pattern that commits an event record in the same database transaction as the source change, then publishes it separately. It makes source and event-record persistence atomic; consumers still need retry, duplicate and ordering handling.
An open-source change data capture platform that reads database change logs and publishes each row change as an event.

PostgreSQL replication of logical data changes using publication and subscription rules. It uses logical decoding to extract row changes from WAL; logical decoding also supports other consumers such as change-data-capture tools, so decoding and replication are distinct stages.

How out of date a copy or summary is compared with its source, for example a cache, replica, materialised view or the planner's statistics. A materialised view reflects the source snapshot used by its last successful refresh; freshness depends on subsequent source changes, not refresh age alone.
A redundant copy gradually disagreeing with its source because some change was not propagated, for example through a bug, a manual fix or a restore. Reconciliation checks find it.
The delay between a change committing on the primary database and appearing on a replica that is replaying its write-ahead log.

In PostgreSQL, an obsolete stored row version that no relevant transaction or retained snapshot can need. VACUUM or eligible heap-page pruning can reclaim its storage; cleanup does not always wait for a VACUUM command.

Heap-only tuple update: a PostgreSQL optimisation avoiding new ordinary index entries when updated columns are not referenced by ordinary indexes and the new row version fits on the same heap page. PostgreSQL 16–18 allow changes to columns referenced only by summarising indexes such as BRIN, whose summaries may still need updates.
A distributed search engine for full-text search and analytics, often fed from a primary database as a derived, eventually consistent copy.
A PostgreSQL extension that runs SQL on a cron-style schedule inside the database, for example to refresh a materialised view every 15 minutes.
PostgreSQL's built-in procedural language for writing functions and trigger functions, with variables, loops and conditions around SQL statements.
A copy allowed to lag that converges once source updates stop, assuming delivery and application eventually succeed. A failed relay or missing retained events can prevent convergence until repaired.
Working out, with domain experts and before writing any DDL, what things exist in a domain, how they relate and which rules always hold.

The entity–relationship model, introduced by Peter Chen in 1976: a model of entity types, their attributes and relationships, with cardinality and participation constraints. Mapping rules produce relational tables, but additional constraints and dependency checks may still be needed.
A kind of thing with its own identity in an ER model, such as Artist or User. Each instance is an entity.
One instance of an entity type in an ER model: a distinct thing the database records facts about, such as one particular artist.
An ER attribute made of parts, such as an address of street, city and postcode. When mapped to tables it is flattened into one column per part.
An ER attribute that can hold several values for one entity, such as an artist's genres. It maps to its own table keyed by owner plus value.
example: artist_genre(artist_id, genre) with primary key (artist_id, genre).

definition: An ER attribute that holds exactly one value per entity, such as an album's title.
An ER attribute that can be computed from others, such as age from birth date. It is usually computed in queries rather than stored.
An ER attribute (or set of attributes) that identifies each entity of a type, playing the role of a candidate key.
The key attribute or attributes that distinguish one entity from another in an ER model. Mapped to a table, it becomes the primary key.
An association between entity types in an ER model, such as a User creates a Playlist. It can have its own attributes.
The maximum number of entities on each side of a relationship: one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:N) or many-to-many (M:N). It decides where the foreign key goes.
example: Artist–Album is 1:N if each album has one artist, M:N if collaborations are allowed.

definition: The minimum side of an ER relationship: total participation means every entity must take part (minimum one), while partial participation allows none. NOT NULL on a foreign key enforces the referencing-side minimum; a parent-side minimum needs additional enforcement.
example: Every album must have an artist (total); an artist may have no albums yet (partial).

definition: A common ER diagram notation that marks each end of a relationship line with its minimum (a circle for zero, a bar for one) and maximum (a bar for one, a three-pronged "crow's foot" for many).
example: ||----o< reads "exactly one to zero or many".

definition: An entity or table that represents a many-to-many relationship, holding the keys of both sides plus any attributes of the relationship itself. Also called a junction table.
example: enrolment(student_id, course_id, grade).

definition: An entity type that can be identified by its own attributes alone. It maps to a table whose primary key is its identifier.
An entity type that can only be identified relative to an owner entity: its key is the owner's key plus a partial key.
example: Track 3 only means something within a given album: key (album_id, track_no).

definition: The entity that a weak entity depends on for identification and existence.
example: An album is the owner of its tracks.

definition: The attribute or attribute set of a weak entity that distinguishes it among entities with the same owner, but not globally.
example: room_no is a partial key: room 101 exists in both Main and Annex.

definition: A rule that one entity may not exist without a related owner. A non-null foreign key enforces the reference; deletion can be rejected or cascaded according to the intended lifecycle.

A relationship involving three entity types at once, such as a supplier providing a part to a project. Replacing it with pairwise relationships is safe only when a domain constraint guarantees that joining the pairs reconstructs exactly the original triples.
example: Supplier S supplies part P to project J.

definition: ER modelling of inheritance: a supertype (such as Payment) has subtypes (CardPayment, BankTransfer) that add their own attributes. Specialisation can be disjoint or overlapping, and total or partial.
Disjoint subtypes mean an entity can belong to at most one subtype; overlapping means it may belong to several. Combined with total specialisation, disjoint means exactly one.
A column, such as kind, that records which subtype a row belongs to in single-table inheritance.
Mapping a type hierarchy to one table with a discriminator. Columns specific to absent subtypes permit NULL, while checks require or exclude values according to the discriminator.

Mapping a type hierarchy to a parent table and tables for subtypes sharing its primary key. Subtype columns can have ordinary NOT NULL constraints; separate rules are needed to ensure every parent has exactly one subtype when membership is total and disjoint.
example: payment(payment_id, amount) plus card_payment(payment_id PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES payment, …).

definition: Mapping each concrete subtype to its own complete table. Queries over all subtypes need UNION ALL, and nothing keeps ids unique across the tables.

A PostgreSQL feature where a child table inherits columns and some constraints from a parent. Unique and foreign-key constraints do not enforce uniqueness or references across the whole inheritance hierarchy.
Martin Fowler's 2002 book cataloguing patterns for enterprise software, including the single-, class- and concrete-table inheritance mappings.
A reference whose target table depends on another column (a type plus an id), as Rails supports. No ordinary foreign key can enforce it, so orphaned references can build up.
example: comment(commentable_type, commentable_id) pointing at photos or videos.

definition: A web application framework for the Ruby language, whose ORM (Active Record) makes polymorphic associations easy to declare.
A design with one nullable foreign key per possible target table plus a CHECK that exactly one is set, so every reference is enforced.
example: CHECK (num_nonnulls(photo_id, video_id) = 1).

definition: A PostgreSQL function that returns how many of its arguments are not NULL.
example: num_nonnulls(1, NULL, 3) returns 2.

definition: Entity–attribute–value modelling stores attributes as data rows rather than a fixed column per attribute. A generic untyped value column weakens per-attribute types and required-value rules; typed variants can restore some constraints at extra complexity.
A six-digit UK bank routing identifier used with an account number. It is a subtype-specific field in the bank-transfer modelling example, rather than an identifier for all payments.

A country identifier defined by ISO 3166, for example GB for the United Kingdom. Choose whether a standard code has the stability and historical identity semantics required before using it as a natural key.
A three-letter code for a currency from ISO 4217, such as GBP for the pound sterling.
An FD whose right side includes at least one attribute outside its determinant. It expresses a restriction beyond the trivial fact that an attribute set determines its own subsets.
An attribute belonging to no candidate key. Dependencies on such attributes receive stricter treatment in 2NF and 3NF than dependencies on prime attributes.
An ER relationship connecting two entity types. Three pairwise binary relationships need not preserve the meaning of one ternary relationship.
A PostgreSQL table scan in which cooperating processes divide the work. Its result still has no guaranteed order without ORDER BY.
Changing a database schema while application traffic continues. Compatible deployment stages, backfill and validation keep old and new application versions working during the change.

A transaction’s database changes commit together or are undone together. Reading multiple statements under Read Committed can straddle a commit, so consistent comparison still needs a suitable snapshot.
Literal course labels in the synthetic student fixture: DB is Databases, OS is Operating Systems and LA is Linear Algebra. They are stored course-code values rather than host-system claims.
The ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code for the United Kingdom. Here GB is a country label, rather than a unit of storage.
An identifier generated to distinguish database entities rather than taken from a domain attribute. It does not remove the need to enforce natural business uniqueness.

An UPDATE that changes a stored count relative to its current value. PostgreSQL serialises conflicting writers on the row, avoiding the lost increment caused by an unlocked application read followed by an absolute write.
Updating many stored copies after one source fact changes. Its cost depends on how many rows are copied and the work required for each update.
Comparing a stored copy or summary with the authoritative source to detect missed or incorrect maintenance. For example, compare a saved comment count with an actual COUNT over comments.

A PostgreSQL materialised-view refresh mode that allows ordinary SELECT readers to continue. It requires a populated view and a qualifying unique index on columns covering every row; one refresh at a time may run on that view.

A decomposition for which joining the projections can produce additional tuples for a legal original relation. Projection forgets which combinations were absent; the larger reconstructed join therefore represents lost information.
A column constraint testing whether a value lies in its allowed range. In PostgreSQL, CHECK accepts UNKNOWN, so NOT NULL is also needed when missing values are forbidden.
A statement template interpreted as true or false for each permitted tuple in the classical null-free relational model. SQL predicates instead can evaluate to UNKNOWN because SQL also has NULL.

A constraint saying that tuples equal on one attribute set must also be equal on another, in every legal relation state. A complete key determines every attribute; arbitrary determinants need not be keys.
A named component of a relational heading, with an assigned domain of permitted values. In an ER model, an attribute describes an entity or relationship before the model is mapped to columns.
An attribute that can be removed from an FD’s determinant while keeping the whole FD set equivalent. Attribute closure tests whether the reduced determinant can already derive the right side.

An ER attribute treated as one conceptual value rather than split into component attributes, such as an album title. A composite address instead has separate street, city and postcode attributes in that model.
An attribute recorded directly as source data instead of being computed from other attributes. Birth date is usually stored, while current age is derived from birth date and the current date.

One stored version of a PostgreSQL row under multiversion concurrency control. An UPDATE creates a new version; the old version can remain visible to older snapshots until it is no longer needed and can be reclaimed. This stored representation is distinct from a tuple in relational theory.

An incoming change older than a version already applied to the same entity. A conditional write can reject it using reliable version or ordering information; a larger numeric data value alone does not establish that an update is newer.
